meta: Omphale lounges at the center while Hercules, her slave and lover, wears his lion pelt in Luigi Garzi's painting of about 1700 to 1710.
about: Omphale, queen of Lydia, lounges at the center of this lush pleasure scene. She had bought Hercules as a slave and lover, and he stands at the left in his lion pelt. He served her for three years, clearing the land of robbers and pests and fathering at least three of her sons. Luigi Garzi painted the mythological picture around 1700 to 1710, and it is in the Getty.

meta: Tobias and the Angel, a Pollaiuolo panel of about 1465 to 1470 with a small white dog, now in Turin.
about: This oil on panel by Antonio and Piero del Pollaiuolo, made around 1465 to 1470, is in the Galleria Sabauda in Turin. It was probably the first of a series of Florentine paintings of Tobias and the Angel with similar features, among them a wide landscape, a small fluffy white dog and a very young, very expensively dressed Tobias. Vasari mentioned it hanging on a pillar of the church of Orsanmichele in Florence.

meta: The Hymn to the Virgin, In Thee Rejoiceth, by the Cretan painter Theodore Poulakis, in tempera and gold leaf.
about: In Thee Rejoiceth is a tempera and gold leaf painting by Theodore Poulakis, with the Virgin Mary as its central figure. It is a tribute to her. Poulakis came from Chania in Crete and worked in the Ionian islands and Venice in the second half of the 17th century. He was a member of the Cretan school and the father of the Heptanese school, and about 130 paintings are attributed to him. His version follows an earlier work by Klontzas.

meta: Count d'Arjuzon plays the violin and his wife the guitar by open French windows in Achille-Louis Martinet's salon scene, about 1810.
about: In this small genre scene the Count d'Arjuzon plays the violin and his wife the guitar in front of open French windows. Pale blue walls and bare parquet floors set off the portrait paintings and the blue armchairs in the Louis XVI style. A globe stands on a corner table to the right of the windows, and a white flowering plant sits on a draped table just in front of it. Achille-Louis Martinet made the picture around 1810.

meta: A miniature of a gentleman with the initials J. B. by Benjamin Trott, once attributed to Raphaelle Peale.
about: On the back of this miniature the initials JB are monogrammed in gold over hairwork, the only clue to who the sitter was. The piece was first attributed to Raphaelle Peale of the Philadelphia family of painters, but it was later found to be the work of Benjamin Trott, around 1790.

meta: A lone man walks a zigzag path by the water while geese fly over distant mountains in Ma Lin's album leaf of the mid-1200s.
about: Most of the elements of this minimalist landscape sit in the lower right foreground. A lone gentleman strolls along a zigzagging path by the water, and his staff points the eye to geese flying over distant mountains. The soft, wet marshland suggests spring in Jiangnan. With the geese, the museum says, the album leaf evokes a poem about geese about to return in the spring fields and fish sinking under chilly water. Ma Lin made it in the mid-1200s.

meta: Cornelis Jansz Meyer, hydraulic engineer, sits at a table with a globe and an open book in a portrait by Abraham van den Hecken.
about: Cornelis Jansz Meyer, a hydraulic engineer, sits full-length in a chair beside a table draped with a large Persian carpet. An open book and a terrestrial globe stand on the table. Abraham van den Hecken painted the portrait, which the catalog dates to 1650.

meta: Mrs. John Jordan Jr. in a sheer dress with a locket, a miniature by John Henry Brown, about 1840.
about: Nothing is known about this woman, who wears a simple dress of sheer fabric with a small locket at her throat. The museum notes that the locket may hold a miniature, since nineteenth-century artists often showed sitters wearing a token like the one being painted. John Henry Brown made the portrait around 1840.

meta: Joseph Paelinck's self-portrait of about 1812 as a dandy in a velvet-collared box-coat, after his training with David.
about: Joseph Paelinck was born in a small Belgian village and won a scholarship to Paris, where he worked with Jacques-Louis David. He later went to Rome to study ancient art and join its lively international scene. Here he shows himself as a dandy in subtly colored fashionable clothes. Over his black suit he wears a box-coat, a garment with a wide velvet collar that began with coachmen but was popular among artists in Rome in the early 19th century.
credit_line: Gift of Elisabeth Ireland and Robert Livingston Ireland Jr., in memory of their mother, Mrs. Perry W. Harvey

meta: A design for a chimney piece with alternative suggestions for the two halves, by Nicolas Pineau, about 1700.
about: The left half of this design includes a candle bracket showing a child holding two scrolls topped by sockets, a medallion with the bust of a woman under a canopy, and a painting of a woman with two children, one of them Cupid. The right half has sparser decoration. Plans of the mantelpiece are in the bottom margin. Nicolas Pineau made the design around 1700.

meta: Geese, ducks and a heron by the water with a frog, butterflies and a ruined tower, painted by Gijsbert Gillisz de Hondecoeter in 1652.
about: Geese and ducks stand at the water's edge with a heron. A frog sits among the foliage in the foreground, butterflies and dragonflies fly, and a river landscape with a ruined tower lies behind. Gijsbert Gillisz de Hondecoeter painted these waterfowl in 1652.

meta: A sheet from a drawing book with two pitchers and a bowl, the handle of one made of two snakes, by Giuseppe Valadier.
about: Three vessels form a group on this sheet from a drawing book. A pitcher with a handle made of two snakes stands in front and partly covers the others. Both pitchers face left, and the bowl is low. Parts of the design are only lightly sketched. The sheet is by Giuseppe Valadier.

meta: A courtier, possibly Khan Alam, holds a spinel and a Deccan sword in Govardhan's Mughal portrait of about 1605 to 1610.
about: The Mughal emperor Akbar ordered likenesses of the grandees of his realm, and his court historian said an immense album was formed in which the dead received new life. Akbar's son Jahangir kept up the tradition. This courtier, possibly Khan Alam, wears a fur-trimmed, fringed velvet coat over a belted white tunic and striped pants, typical Mughal dress derived from their nomadic Central Asian roots. He holds a spinel and a Deccan sword. Govardhan painted it around 1605 to 1610.
credit_line: Gift in honor of Madeline Neves Clapp; Gift of Mrs. Henry White Cannon by exchange; Bequest of Louise T. Cooper; Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund; From the Catherine and Ralph Benkaim Collection
